title: Beyond Truthfulness: Evaluating Honesty in Large Language Models
claim: Models may state things contradicting their beliefs under pressure, undermining trust; our benchmark checks statement-belief consistency across diverse high-stakes domains.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right with arrow; thought-bubble vs speech-box cartoon, dataset stack
description: The left panel shows a cartoon robot with a purple thought bubble labeled "Belief" and an orange speech box labeled "Statement". A double arrow and an equals sign with a question mark sit between them, asking whether the two match. A small red/green "MASK" bar sits under the robot. Below, a rounded gray box reads "If models lie, we may not get reliable answers to...". It lists four domains with icons, each paired with an example question: AI Oversight, Legal Harms, Financial and Privacy. A black arrow leads right to a stacked-card dataset schematic. Its top half has two boxes: an orange "Prompt for Pressuring Model to Lie" and a purple "Prompts for Eliciting Beliefs from Model". Beneath them is a blue "Ground Truth Label" box. At the bottom, four lab logos (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, DeepSeek) each have a red/green MASK score bar.
caption: Increasingly powerful AI systems should consistently choose to be honest, even if incentivized or pressured to lie. Our MASK evaluation verifies consistency between statements and beliefs, creating a valid construct for understanding model lying.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable and agentic, the requirement for trust in their outputs grows significantly, yet at the same time concerns have been mounting that models may learn to lie in pursuit of their goals. To address these concerns, a body of work has emerged around the notion of "honesty" in LLMs, along with interventions aimed at mitigating deceptive behaviors. However, some benchmarks claiming to measure honesty in fact simply measure accuracy—the correctness of a model's beliefs—in disguise. Moreover, no benchmarks currently exist for directly measuring whether language models contradict a robustly elicited belief under pressure. In this work, we introduce a realistic, large-scale human-curated dataset for directly measuring lies of commission, allowing us to disentangle accuracy from honesty. Across a diverse set of LLMs, we find that while larger models obtain higher accuracy on our benchmark, they do not become more honest. Surprisingly, most frontier LLMs obtain high scores on truthfulness benchmarks yet exhibit a substantial propensity to lie under pressure, resulting in low scores on our benchmark. We find that simple methods, such as representation engineering interventions, can improve honesty. These results underscore the growing need for robust evaluations and effective interventions to ensure LLMs remain trustworthy.
